Excellence, excellencies, High Commissioner for Human Rights, The first session of the 37th extraordinary meeting of the Human Rights Council is hereby declared open. Please allow me at the outset to recall some basic issues. On the 3rd of February in the evening, I received a call for a special session of the Council concerning the situation of human rights in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. This request was submitted by the Permanent Representative of the Democratic Republic of Congo and has received the support of 27 Member States of the Council. They are South Africa, Algeria, Germany, Belgium, Bulgaria, Burundi, Chile, Cyprus, Colombia, Costa Rica, Spain, France, Ghana, Marshall Islands, Iceland, Japan, Kyrgyzstan, North Macedonia, Malawi, Morocco, the Netherlands, the Republic of Korea, the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Dominican Republic, Romania, Switzerland and the Czech Republic. This request has also been supported by 21 observer states to the Council, who are Australia, Austria, Croatia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Poland, Portugal, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, Slovakia, Slovenia and Sweden. To date, Albania, Canada, Cote d'Ivoire, Maldives, Mexico, Montenegro, Norway and Uruguay have also expressed their support for this special session. The request to convene this special session was officially communicated by the secretariat to all United Nations member states on the fourth of February. The information has also been made available to specialized institutions, other intergovernmental organizations, national human rights institutions, as well as non-governmental organizations with consultative status to the ECOSOC. in accordance with the Council's rules of procedure. The online inscription system for speakers was opened on Wednesday, the 5th of February at 2 p.m., remained open until 6 p.m. yesterday. Excellencies, I now give the floor to Mr. Volker Turk, High Commissioner for Human Rights, for his statement. High Commissioner, you have the floor.

Thank you very much, President. Minister for Communication of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Excellencies, I've been following the human rights situation in the Democratic Republic of Congo for many years, and I have to say that I've always been tremendously worried by it. I've been to Goma on at least five occasions when holding other posts. When I visited the country in April 2024, I met victims of this dreadful conflict. They included women who had been the victims of sexual violence. My office has been raising alarm about this crisis for a long time, and I'm deeply disturbed when I see the escalation of violence occurring once again. Since the start of the year, the M23 armed group supported by the Rwanda Defense Forces has stepped up its offensive in the provinces of North Kivu and South Kivu, and tensions are currently rising in South Kivu. If nothing is done, then the worst could still be yet to come for the inhabitants of the eastern part of the country but also in people living beyond the drc's borders there have been attacks by the M23 and their allies heavy Weaponry has been used in populated areas and there's been intense fighting with the drc's Armed Forces and their allies this is all very worrying when it comes to respect for human rights and international humanitarian law and I condemn all violations and abuse. Once again in this crushing conflict, civilians have been trapped in escalating violence. Since the 26th of January, around 3,000 people have lost their lives and 2,880 have been wounded. The real figures are probably a lot higher. In Goma on the 27th of January two hospitals were bombed. This killed and wounded many patients including women and children. I am horrified by the spread of sexual violence. This is an appalling feature of this conflict and has been for a long time. And it could get worse in the current circumstances. According to the judicial authorities, when there was the mass prison break from Muzenza prison in Goma on the 27th January, at least 165 female prisoners were raped. Most of them were killed thereafter in a fire, the circumstances of which remain unclear. In addition, my team is currently checking multiple allegations of rape, gang rape, and sexual slavery throughout the conflict zones. Hundreds of human rights defenders, journalists, and civil society activists have reported to my office that they've been threatened or being searched for by the M23 and Rwandan forces. We have also been providing protection to endangered judicial authorities. I'm really worried and concerned about the proliferation of weapons and the high risk of forced conscription and recruitment of children. Credible reports indicate that M23 has bombed electricity transmission towers that enable water to be supplied to civilians. This fighting has exacerbated a terrible humanitarian crisis which is the upshot of persistent human rights violations. Since the start of January, over half a million people have been displaced. This is in addition to the already displaced 6.4 million people. I am also disturbed at the allegations of forced returns of thousands of displaced people to their homes in North and South Kivu without any guarantee of their safety or access to basic services. This is therefore return without dignity. Goma airport, which is so important for humanitarian aid, was rendered inoperable by the M23 and Rwandan forces. Warehouses belonging to the MONUSCO mission and humanitarian organisations have been looted. Excellencies, the risk of violence escalating throughout the sub-region has never been higher. All those with influence over the parties involved, be they states or non-state actors, must step up their efforts to avert a conflagration and to support peace processes. It's also vital that we analyze the political economy of this conflict. I've always been struck by the fact that people in eastern DRC face terrible suffering. Whilst many of the products that we consume or use, such as mobile phones, are produced using minerals from the east of the country, so we're all implicated. Those who think they can reach a solution to violence through military means are wrong. An even deeper and wider conflict would have even more devastating consequences for civilians. I call on all parties to lay down their weapons and to resume dialogue within the framework of the Luanda-Nairobi processes. I hope that today's meeting in Dar es Salaam will produce tangible results. We must ensure that the meaningful participation of women in these processes is guaranteed. In the meantime, all parties to conflict must respect international human rights law and international humanitarian law. The M23 Rwandan forces and all those supporting them must facilitate access for humanitarian aid. Air, land and lake routes must be reopened to establish humanitarian corridors and guarantee the safety of humanitarian actors. In these circumstances, it is crucial to establish the facts and bring perpetrators of offences to justice. We must therefore open up an independent, impartial investigation into human rights violations and abuses and violations of international humanitarian law committed by all parties. I offer my office's support in this regard. I also welcome this week's appeal by the International Criminal Court to all parties concerned to submit information on the situation in the DRC. And I reiterate the United Nations Secretary-General's call to the Rwanda Defense Forces to cease all support for the M23 and to withdraw their soldiers from the DRC. The military path is not the answer to the political, social, and economic challenges which are at the root of this conflict, including the illegal exploitation of natural resources. In line with the principles of due diligence, states must ensure that any support, financial or otherwise, does not fuel serious human rights violations. Corruption within state institutions must also be tackled. Such institutions must be made efficient and social cohesion restored throughout the country. Press freedom and civic space must be preserved. Hate speech and other Forms of incitement to discrimination and violence only stoke conflict and political tension. They're completely unacceptable and ways must be found to confront them. I call on political and community leaders to play a positive role in promoting social cohesion. Excellencies, the Congolese people have been suffering terribly for decades. I express my full solidarity with the victims, their families and human rights defenders. How many more innocent lives must be lost before sufficient political will is galvanised to resolve this crisis? All those with influence must act urgently to put an end to this tragic situation. I thank you.

I thank you for that statement, High Commissioner. I would now like to give the floor to Mr. Surya Dever, Chair of the Coordinating Committee for Special Procedures via video conference. You have the floor, sir.

Thank you, Mr. President, excellencies, and distinguished delegates. I have the honor of addressing the Human Rights Council today on behalf of the Coordination Committee of the UN Special Procedures. We welcome the decision to convene a special session on the human rights situation in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, given the escalating crisis and the grave human rights violations affecting civilians, particularly North and South Kivu. As highlighted in the recent press release issued by several special procedure mandate holders yesterday, we have been closely monitoring the situation in the DRC. The intensification of hostilities, particularly in North Kivu, following the renewed offensive by the Rwandan-backed M23 armed groups has led to widespread violence, forced displacement, and serious violations of international human rights and humanitarian law. The scale of the violence has reached unprecedented levels. Reports indicate that entire communities have been uprooted, with families forced to flee their homes in search of safety. The humanitarian consequences are devastating, as those displaced often find themselves with no access to shelter, water, sanitation, food, medical care, or education. Women and children are particularly at risk, facing heightened exposure to gender-based violence and trafficking for purposes of sexual slavery. We are also concerned at the devastating impact on children who are at serious risk of all six grave violations against children in armed conflict. In recent weeks, over 700,000 individuals have been displaced due to these hostilities, adding to the already staggering figure of 6.7 million internally displaced persons in the DRC, as also mentioned by the High Commissioner. The indiscriminate bombardment of densely populated areas, including displacement camps, has resulted in mass civilian casualties and triggered panic and forced returns under unsafe conditions. There are also reports of summary executions and civilians being subjected to forced conscription and labor. Reports indicate that the M23 movement has systematically dismantled displacement sites in areas under its control, forcing individuals to return to their areas of origin without guarantees of safety or dignity. Thus, displacement sites, which should offer refuge, have instead become sites of renewed violence. Hospitals in the region are overwhelmed, struggling to cope up with the influx of injured civilians amid shortages of medical supplies, personal and essential medicines. Moreover, humanitarian access to conflict-affected areas remains severely restricted, with aid workers facing security threats, looting of relief supplies, and targeted attacks on humanitarian facilities. This has significantly hindered the delivery of life-saving assistance. The collapse of infrastructure in affected regions has severely disrupted essential services, including education and healthcare. The destruction of medical facilities has left countless individuals without access to urgent medical care. This is particularly concerning for vulnerable populations, including indigenous Pygmy peoples, persons with disabilities, older persons, and victims of conflict-related sexual violence, who face significant barriers in accessing assistance. Mr. President, we reiterate our urgent call for all parties to the conflict to adhere to their obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law. We call for the immediate cessation of attacks against civilians, the protection of civilian infrastructure, and unimpeded access for humanitarian actors to deliver assistance to those in need. We also call on all parties involved in the conflict to refrain from supporting or using mercenary-related actors. We echo the Secretary-General's appeal for Rwanda to cease support for M23 and withdraw from the DRC territory. The forced return of internally displaced persons to their areas of origin must end. Their right to voluntary, safe, and dignified solutions must be upheld in accordance with international law. Equally, the targeting of human rights defenders, ethnic minorities, journalists, and humanitarian workers must stop. The international community has a moral and legal obligation to act decisively. We urge member states to increase humanitarian funding to ensure the continued provision of essential services and assistance to displaced populations. In addition, Coordinated diplomatic efforts must be intensified to support peace negotiations and to hold accountable those responsible for violations of international human rights and humanitarian law. We also call upon regional actors, the international community, and businesses to intensify efforts to achieve a peaceful resolution to the crisis and prevent further deterioration of the situation. Finally, we stress the need for independent investigations into all reported human rights violations, including attacks on civilians, sexual and gender-based violence, and other abuses perpetrated during the conflict. Establishing robust accountability mechanisms is critical to preventing impunity and ensuring justice for victims. Mr. President, the Special Procedures remain committed to working with the Council, the High Commissioner, regional human rights bodies, and other relevant stakeholders to monitor, report on, and provide advice regarding measures to address the human rights situations in the DRC. We stand ready to employ all available tools, including conducting country visits and offering technical assistance. We urge the DRC to facilitate pending country visits by mandate holders, including the Special Rapporteur on the human rights of internally displaced persons and the Special Rapporteur on trafficking in persons. The gravity of the situation demands urgent and sustained international engagement. The people of the DRC cannot afford further inaction. They need immediate relief. protection, and a path towards sustainable peace, inclusive development, and justice. As reaffirmed by the Pact for the Future, sustainable development, peace and security, and human rights are interlinked and mutually reinforcing pillars of the United Nations. We cannot have one without the others. I thank you, Mr. President.

Yes, thank you for your statement, Your Excellency. We're waiting for Ms. Bintou Keita to arrive. She's the special representative of the Secretary General. in the Democratic Republic of Congo and head of the United Nations Organisation Stabilisation Mission in the country. She has just arrived at Geneva airport and as soon as she gets here I will give her the floor. In line with our habitual practice, I will give the floor now to the representatives of the concerned countries. Excellency, Minister, you have the floor for five minutes.

President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, Members of the Human Rights Council, the Democratic Republic of Congo expresses its deep gratitude to the Human Rights Council for holding this special session, which has been co-sponsored by over 30 Member States and 22 Observer States. This meeting is a response to the urgent situation of mass human rights violations and attacks on civilians in North and South Kivu, which are the result of attacks and offensives by the Rwandan Defence Forces and their M23 and AFC proxies. Indiscriminate bombing against IDP camps and populated areas have compounded A catastrophic humanitarian situation. These attacks have deliberately targeted vulnerable people, which is a flagrant violation of the principles of humanity, distinction, precaution, proportionality and preventing unnecessary suffering. The Rwanda Defence Forces and their proxies have transformed areas of shelter into military targets. imperiling the lives of thousands of innocent people, including women and children. In Goma, where there is no water, electricity, the principles of international humanitarian laws have been systematically violated. There's been indiscriminate bombing against residential areas causing mass... displacement of people and there have been attacks against IDP camps. This is particularly alarming because people are already very vulnerable and they have been trapped between the Rwandan forces and their M23 proxies have also been supported by foreign actors. According to the UN, the offensive which led to the occupation of Goma, at least 3,000 people were killed and a further 3,000 were wounded. Attacks against civilians and the forced displacement of people, attacks against IDP camps reflect unacceptable brutality which is compounded by unspeakable atrocities, notably murders, the rape of at least 200 women, massacres. forced conscription of children taken to Rutshuru training camps and others. By actively supporting the armed groups, Rwanda is directly responsible for violations which has exposed civilians to unspeakable suffering. Peacekeeping forces with the Security Council mandate, particularly MONUSCO, as well as humanitarian facilities have been targeted on a number of occasions. This has undermined their ability to protect civilians in a hostile environment. We also deplore the attacks against the SADC regional forces, which have been working tirelessly for regional stability. President, in view of this situation, the Democratic Republic of Congo calls for the establishment of an international commission of inquiry to examine human rights violations committed in my country. This commission must have a mandate to establish the truth as to who is responsible for these crimes and to provide recommendations for holding them accountable. We also call for tangible measures to be adopted to prevent future violations of this nature. It's vital that we strengthen monitoring and early warning mechanisms and to ensure better coordination between MONUSCO, Congolese security forces and regional actors in order to protect civilians and prevent further escalations of violence. Furthermore, it's vital today that we ensure immediate and unfettered humanitarian access in order to better care for the thousands of injured, evacuate the most seriously injured and reduce the risk of the spread of epidemics such as cholera and mpox in a city which has already been traumatized and where corpses litter many streets. We firmly reject the involvement of certain states, particularly Rwanda. They've provided logistical, military and financial support to armed groups operating on our territory. Rwanda's support for M23, which has been documented on a number of occasions, including by the UN Security Council group of experts, has stoked violence in the east of our country for over 30 years, compounding the war for reasons linked to the exploitation of Congo's strategic mineral resources. We call upon the Council to hold Rwanda accountable for its war crimes and crimes against humanity, particularly the forced displacement of people and their replacement by others, as well as by appointing new administrative authorities with a view to permanently occupying these territories. It's vital that international pressure be applied to Rwanda so that it immediately puts a stop to its support for the armed groups and… immediately withdraws from Congolese territory president the Democratic Republic of Congo remains steadfastly committed to searching for peace and stability we reiterate that we stand ready to work constructively with all regional international actors but it's absolutely vital the international community firmly supports our efforts to put a stop to this crisis and to put an end to the suffering of our people living in the east of our country thus we reiterate our call for Rwanda to act responsibly and take immediate measures to put a stop to its support to armed groups. A consensual adoption of the resolution would be a sign of solidarity for the millions of Congolese people living under Rwandan occupation today. I thank you for your attention, President. Thank you.

I'd like to thank you for your statement and I would now like to give the floor to the distinguished representative of Rwanda for his statement as a concerned country. Excellency, you have five minutes.

Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to start by thanking the High Commissioner for the oral statement on the situation in the eastern DRC, which persistently constitutes a security threat to the Great Lakes region. and Rwanda in particular. The current session is called for at a time when the situation in the eastern DRC is evolving rapidly. The Eastern African Community Summit of 29th January and the South African Development Summit of 31st January 2025 have convened a summit to discuss today and tomorrow with a view to holding a frank discussion on this crisis and in the hope of finding a lasting solution to the crisis. Therefore, we should give a chance to this important regional initiative to bear fruits before preempting their outcome and attempting to feed the ongoing discussions in the relevant UN bodies. This reminds us of the fate of the EAC regional force, that made a stride in imposing ceasefire and accompanying the peace process from March to September 2023, during which the M23 relinquished 8% of the territory it was previously holding. But before this process could be completed, the DRC unilaterally decided to expel the force, replacing it with the SADC with an offensive mandate in pursuit of a military solution. Rwanda raised concerns about the substitution of the EAC force, a troop-keeping force, with the SADC, an offensive force. SADC is now part of the Kinshasa-led military coalition, which includes the UN-sanctioned genocide militia FDLR, Burundi forces, European mercenaries, with logistical and operational support by the UN. Those concerns are now proven right as we unfortunately witness the result of imposing a military solution to a political problem. Mr. President, these root causes we shall repeat time and again, on the one hand, the preservation of the FDLR, a group that committed genocide in Rwanda in 1994, fled to the DRC where they now pose an existential threat to our security and continue spreading their genocidal ideology. On the other hand, the marginalization of Kinyarwanda-speaking Congolese community, particularly Tutsi, by the government of DRC. Everyone here in this session recalls the Congolese citizens were abominably massacred, lashed, burned, and cannibalized for looking Tutsi. Yet there was no urgent meeting of, there was no urgent meeting or a special session of this, on this issue. There was no condemnation of the DRC top leadership who used hate speech for electoral purposes and justified the prosecution of a portion of its own citizens. Furthermore, there was no special session of this council when, in April 2024, the UN Special Advisor on the Prevention of Genocide, Ms. Alice Wairum Ondiruti, warned about the risk factors for genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity in the eastern DRC. Mr. President, We categorically oppose the DRC attempts to portray Rwanda as being responsible for the instability in the eastern DRC. It is a well-known deflection tactic used to escape being accountable for the atrocities Kinshasa and its allied armed group are inflicting on their own citizens. What is clear, however, is the imminent threat the current situation poses to Rwanda. Following the fall of Goma, new evidence has come in light regarding an imminent large-scale attack against Rwanda. The Kinshasa-backed coalition has stockpiled a large number of weapons and military equipment near Rwanda's border, mostly in or around the Goma airport. These weapons include rockets, kamikaze drones, heavy artillery guns capable to shoot precisely within the Rwandan territory. The weapons were not turned at the threat of operations, at the theater of operations against the M23, rather they were pointed directly at Rwanda. I would like to recall that on January 26, 2025, retreating DRC forces fired at Rwanda, causing tragic loss of 16 Rwandan lives and injury of 161 civilians. These shelling were deliberate.
I'm sorry, I ask you to come to the conclusion of your statement.

And they could strongly be condemned. Rwanda will not wait for the threat to materialize, and this is why our country maintain proportional, punctual, and dynamic measures to the border to prevent any spillover of this kind and respond appropriately.

Thank you for your declaration.

I now give the floor to Ms. Pinto-Kayta, Special Representative of the Secretary General for the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the representative of MONUSCO.

You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. President of the Human Rights Council, Minister of Communication of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Madam Minister for Human Rights, Madam Minister for Foreign Trade, Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs, Vice Minister of National Affairs, High Commissioner, distinguished members of the Human Rights Council. I thank you for this emergency session on this extremely troubling situation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. I would first and foremost express my condolences to the government and the Congolese people who have been victims of this conflict for 30 years and who continue to live in fear. My thoughts also go to the Blue Helmets and their families who have lost lives, and my thoughts go to those who were injured as well. I welcome those who work with commitment towards a lasting peace in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. I would also like to condemn the attacks and pillaging against the UN. on the 27th of September. I welcome the efforts of the government to bring perpetrators to justice and to prevent any further incidents of this nature. Mr. President, we have witnessed an unprecedented advance of the M23 and the Rwandan forces. The taking of the city of Goma on the 27th of January were preceded by violent clashes. between the RDC forces, the Democratic Republic of the Congo forces and their allies, and on the other side, the Rwandan forces and their allies. There are thousands who were injured. The long term and mid term consequences are alarming. There is a possibility of the resurgence of cholera and mpox, and this also has an effect on the school attendance of children and the risk of sexual violence and gender-based violence due to the clashes. The presence of M23 in the North Kivu, where it occupies four of the six territories, and the taking over of several of the municipalities in the South Kivu have led to mass displacement. Moreover, we note violence, violations and abuse of human rights, deteriorations of services, and an ever-increasingly tenuous access to basic services. The humanitarian situation has drastically declined. The economy of the province of Goma was also affected by the conflict. Agricultural and mining activities, which are the main source of income for the population, as well as for the provincial government, are paralyzed. At the same time, fighting impunity against the serious crimes committed may be impeded due to the damage caused to the judiciary institutions of Goma. It is imperative that emergency measures be taken to stabilize the region, restore peace, and allow for a lasting rebuilding in the region. Mr. President, I recall the need to pursue diplomatic negotiations between the governments of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and of Rwanda, in particular in the context of the Rwanda process. I would like to emphasise the risk of the extension of the conflict throughout the region unless deterrent, compelling measures are taken to stop an escalation of the violence. The unilateral ceasefire announced by the M23 and its partners, the Alliance for the Congo, on 4 February held only for one day and allowed for the presumed strengthening of their positions in the north and south Kivu and the resurgence of intense combats in near the city of Bukavu. These clashes in densely settled areas, including in Goma, have led to devastating consequences on the civilian population. Crime and the increase of popular justice are alarming. There has been a proliferation of weapons abandoned by soldiers and there has been a prison break of the central prison of Goma on the 27th of January.

Forced recruitment and human rights defenders, civil society actors and journalists have also become a major population at risk. monusco continues to receive requests for individual protection from them as well as from judicial authorities under threat and at risk of reprisal from m twenty three in areas under its control. such reprisal must stop immediately. furthermore mis and disinformation are rampant and pose serious risks. The suspension of social networks such as X and TikTok by the Congolese authorities is a serious infringement of the right to information and must be swiftly lifted in line with the statement of the Vice Prime Minister of Interior. In a region with a sensitive history, ethnically motivated attacks remain a serious concern. The United Nations Joint Human Rights Office documented a case of allegedly ethnically motivated lynching in an internally displaced person site, as well as physical and verbal violence against journalists in Goma, in Kalehe, South Kivu. Our Joint Human Rights Office has received reports of physical attacks, abduction and extortion of civilians linked to the perceived ethnicity of the victims. I thus call for unity and social cohesion and encourage the adoption of the draft law against tribalism, racism and xenophobia. I reiterate that the humanitarian situation in Goma is catastrophic. The decomposing bodies collected from the streets of Goma prompted WHO to warn of potential epidemics. Medical personnel are facing electricity cuts and lack fuel for their generators. They work under extremely difficult conditions when ensuring the treatment of patients and the functioning of morgues. I again call on international community to advocate for humanitarian assistance to reach Goma immediately. The rebuilding and reopening of Goma airport, along with the cessation of GPS jamming and spoofing practices, is vital for the evacuation of the wounded and the entry of aid. Hundreds of thousands of displaced people are being forced by M23 to return to their places of origin without any guarantee or humanitarian assistance on their safe and dignified return. Among them are people with chronic diseases such as HIV or tuberculosis. We must ensure the continuation of their life-saving treatment, Mr. President. I would like to end my statement by thanking this Council and the High Commissioner for OHCHR's continuous engagement on the respect of human rights in the DRC. I also acknowledge the pivotal role of Congolese women are playing in advocating for peace and human rights in the DRC, often in the face of immense personal risk. I encourage women's youth and women's groups to coordinate their efforts and stand in solidarity, to support them and all peace actors in the DRC. I look forward to this session taking concrete steps to halt the long-lasting suffering of the Congolese population and pave the way for inclusive and sustainable development. Thank you for your attention.

I thank you for your statement and for your efforts in making the journey to come here to be with us today. We will now begin with the speakers list. Allow me to remind you that the speaking time is limited to two minutes and 30 seconds for members of the Council and one minute and 30 seconds for observer states and other observers. I would ask each speaker to comply with the speaking time. The speakers list will be closed in 15 minutes. We begin by the speakers for the member states of the Council. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Sweden on behalf of a group of countries.

Mr. President, I have the honor to speak on behalf of the Nordic and Baltic countries. Let me start by thanking the High Commissioner and the Special Representative for their clear and compelling briefings. Mr. President, we are deeply concerned about the escalating violence in eastern DRC. We urge the M23 to stop its advance and withdraw immediately. We reiterate that Rwanda must cease its support for the M23 and withdraw its armed forces. We strongly condemn Rwanda's military presence in the DRC as a clear violation of international law, the UN Charter, and the territorial integrity of the Democratic Republic of Congo. And we continue to urge the DRC to cease its cooperation with the FDLR. We are alarmed by reports of widespread violations and abuses of human rights and international humanitarian law by multiple actors. including sexual and gender-based violence, the recruitment and use of child soldiers, and extrajudicial executions. The offensive has deepened the already disastrous humanitarian crisis in eastern DRC. The risk of large numbers of IDPs being caught between the conflicting parties is deeply worrying. All sides must prioritise protection of civilians, ensure safe and unhindered humanitarian access and fully respect their obligations under international law, including human rights law and international humanitarian law. Mr. President, we call for all perpetrators of atrocity crimes to be held accountable. Impunity must not be allowed. We commend the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICC's renewed investigative efforts in the DRC, with a priority focus given to any alleged Rome Statute crimes occurring in eastern DRC since January 2022. We fully support the work of the High Commissioner, as well as the team of international experts on the DRC, whose mandate was renewed at the 57th regular session of the Human Rights Council. In conclusion, Mr. President, we call for a quick resumption of political dialogue and negotiations in the Luanda process, and also reiterate our support to the Nairobi process. We support the need to investigate and document all human rights abuses and violations in eastern Congo and identify those responsible. I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the European Union.

Mr. President, High Commissioner, Albania, Macedonia, Montenegro, Moldova, and Ukraine align themselves with this statement. For decades, the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo has witnessed instability. as well as human rights violations and abuses. The root causes and drivers are complex, multilayered and interlinked. Over the past few weeks, the situation has escalated and led to thousands of deaths and wounded and forced displacement of hundreds of thousands of Congolese civilians. Reports of grave violations and abuses of human rights, including summary executions, demand our immediate attention. In particular, the European Union is appalled by reports of a dramatic increase in cases of conflict related sexual and gender based violence. Furthermore, the recent deadly attacks on peacekeepers whose aim is to protect the civilian population are utterly intolerable and may constitute grave violations of international law. The European Union condemns in the strongest terms the offensive of the M23 supported by the Rwandan armed forces in eastern DRC that led to the occupations of large parts of Congolese territory in North and South Kivu, including the city of Goma. The EU urges the M23 to stop its advance and withdraw immediately. The EU also strongly condemns Rwanda's military presence in the DRC, has a clear violation of international law, the UN charter, the territorial integrity of the drc we call on the rwandan government to respect the territorial integrity of the drc by immediately withdrawing all troops from the territory of the drc and end all forms of support for m twenty three and other non state armed groups. the eu also continues to urge the DRC to cease cooperation with the FDLR and other armed groups and take a decisive stance against hate speech. We call upon all parties to reengage in negotiations and be open for inclusive talks with all. We also call upon all parties to respect international law and to honor their commitments made under the Luanda and Nairobi process. Mr. President, This Council cannot stand idle when international human rights law is being disregarded once again in eastern DRC. All accusations of violations and abuses need to be thoroughly investigated, victims recognised and supported, and all perpetrators need to be held accountable for all their crimes. We therefore support the resolution put forward by the DRC requesting the establishment of an independent fact-finding mission to investigate and document all violations and abuses. of human rights in eastern DRC and identify all those responsible.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Morocco.

Thank you, President, High Commissioner. My delegation would like to extend a warm welcome to the delegation of the friendly and brotherly country of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and we share with that country the feeling of solidarity, compassion and support given the alarming humanitarian situation in the country, given the humanitarian crisis and the risk for the territorial integrity, it is essential to address these issues. And this means that through this session we are holding today, we need to address the underlying issues. So we welcome the resolution of the Security Council on the DRC, as well as the praiseworthy role of the Blue Helmets in this country. of which the Moroccan contingent is a key component, working towards ensuring the stability of this brotherly people.
